title: Cluny (910)
hookLine: a monastery freed from local lords so its monks could pray, and a renewal that spread

lines: A DUKE AND HIS HUNTING LODGE.
A PROMISE NEVER TO TAKE IT BACK.
cards: A duke has land he loves: woods, a river, a lodge where he keeps his hunting dogs. A monk asks him for it.
There's a story people tell about that conversation: the duke protests that the place is full of his hounds, and the monk answers, more or less, drive out the dogs and bring in the monks.
Whether or not it went that way, the duke said yes. Then he signed a charter that did something stranger than giving land away. He promised never to take it back.

teach.h: A LORD COULD OWN A MONASTERY.
teach.b: Here was the problem. A lord who founded a monastery could treat it as his own property: name the abbot, take the rents, lean on it when he needed money. The prayer went on, but someone else held the keys.
Duke William's charter changed that. He gave Cluny to the apostles Peter and Paul and placed it under the protection of the pope in Rome.
The monks, the charter says, are to be under no one's yoke: not his, not his family's, not any earthly power.
No prince, no count, no bishop, not even the pope himself, may seize their goods or set an abbot over them against their will.
When their abbot, Berno, died, the monks would choose the next one themselves, by the Rule of Saint Benedict.

teach.h: FREEDOM FOR THE WORK OF GOD.
teach.b: The freedom wasn't for its own sake. Cluny gave itself to the work of God: long, sung prayer through the day and night, for the living and the dead.
Saint Paul writes, in the Douay-Rheims: "Stand fast, and be not held again under the yoke of bondage." The charter speaks the same language of yokes. Then it spread.
Other houses asked Cluny's abbots to reform them, or were handed over to Cluny, and its way of life went with them. Some later monks thought Cluny had grown too grand.
But the charter's idea outlived the argument: a house of prayer should belong to God, not to whoever owns the land.

how: Benedictine houses today, including those that trace their customs to Cluny, elect their own abbots or abbesses under the Rule of Saint Benedict and keep the hours of prayer as the center of the day.

games.q: you're a duke founding a monastery on your own land. what do you keep for yourself?
o: the right to name the abbot.
nothing: you bind yourself and your heirs to stay out.
games.why: Duke William put Cluny under no one's yoke, his own included, so the monks would be free for the work of God.

practice: Picture tomorrow's first quiet minutes, the ones the phone or the inbox usually takes, and give them a little charter of your own: phone in another room, door closed.
If you pray, that's where prayer can live; if you don't, let those minutes simply be yours, unclaimed.

wordCard.voice: Cluny. A monastery whose founder signed away every claim on it, so its monks could choose their abbot and give themselves to prayer. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: free to pray. Next, the Church tries to make peace without an army. Day seven hundred ninety-eight, done.
